title: A finite group-scheme kernel gives finite scheme-theoretic fibres
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], let $G,H$ be group schemes of finite type over $k$ [def-sc-group-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and let $u:G\to H$ be a homomorphism. Suppose its scheme-theoretic kernel $K=G\times_{H,u,e_H}\operatorname{Spec}k$ is finite over $k$ [def-sc-group-scheme]. For every point $y\in H$, with residue field $\kappa(y)$ [def-weil-residue-field], the scheme-theoretic fibre $G_y=G\times_H\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(y)$ [def-pc-scheme-fibre] is finite over $\kappa(y)$ [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism]. In particular $\dim G_y\leq0$ for topological Krull dimension, with $\dim\varnothing=-\infty$ [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension]. No surjectivity, properness, smoothness, connectedness or equal-dimension hypothesis is imposed.

source.place: Chapter I Proposition 7.1, printed p.32, first proof paragraph (translation of fibres after scalar extension); its fibre argument for finite kernels uses only the group law and finite type, and applies to group schemes over an arbitrary field.

proof.text: Fix $y\in H$, put $F=\kappa(y)$ and $P=G_y$. If $P=\varnothing$, then $P=\operatorname{Spec}(0)$ and its coordinate algebra is the zero, hence finite-dimensional, $F$-module; its dimension is $-\infty$. Otherwise choose a point $z\in P$ and put $L=\kappa(z)$. The residue-field map gives $F\hookrightarrow L$. The canonical map $\operatorname{Spec}L\to P$, followed by $P\to G$, gives $x\in G(L)$ with $u(x)=y_L$. Thus $x$ gives an $L$-point of $P_L=P\times_F\operatorname{Spec}L$; no $F$-rational point is asserted.

source.place: I Proposition 7.1, printed p.32, first proof paragraph: extension of scalars for fibres

proof.text: Write $K_L=K\times_k\operatorname{Spec}L$. Define $t:K_L\to P_L$ by left multiplication by $x$, and $s:P_L\to K_L$ by left multiplication by $x^{-1}$. These are scheme morphisms: form multiplication with the constant section $x$ (respectively its inverse) and use the fibre-product universal property. For $t$, the homomorphism identity gives $u(xa)=u(x)u(a)=y_L e=y_L$ on $K_L$; for $s$ it gives $u(x^{-1}b)=u(x)^{-1}u(b)=y_L^{-1}y_L=e$ on $P_L$. These equalities are identities of morphisms, using the group-scheme diagrams, so the maps factor through the indicated scheme-theoretic fibre products, including their nilpotents. Associativity, unit and inverse give $s(t(a))=x^{-1}(xa)=a$ and $t(s(b))=x(x^{-1}b)=b$ as morphisms. Hence $t$ and $s$ are inverse isomorphisms over $L$.

source.place: I Proposition 7.1, printed p.32: fibres are translates of the kernel after scalar extension; explicit group-law argument

proof.text: The structure map $K_L\to\operatorname{Spec}L$ is the base change of the finite map $K\to\operatorname{Spec}k$, so it is finite by clause (a) of [lem-weil-pbc-finite-morphism-permanence] (Stacks Tag 01WL). The preceding isomorphism over $L$ transfers this to $P_L\to\operatorname{Spec}L$: an isomorphism preserves affineness and identifies the coordinate algebras as $L$-algebras, so their finite-module condition is identical.

The singleton family $\{\operatorname{Spec}L\to\operatorname{Spec}F\}$ is an fpqc covering. Indeed the only stalk map is the field inclusion $F\to L$, which is flat: choose an $F$-basis of $L$, so tensoring with $L$ is a direct sum of copies of the identity functor on $F$-vector spaces and preserves exact sequences. Both spectra have one point and the whole affine source covers the whole affine target, as required by [def-weil-pbc-fpqc-covering]. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-fpqc-descend-finite] (Stacks Tag 02LA) to $P\to\operatorname{Spec}F$ and this covering. Its base change is the finite morphism of the previous step, so $P$ is finite over $F$. This proves the assertion for every $y$, with the empty case already settled.

source.place: Tag 02LA, lemma-descending-property-finite; the singleton covering is checked directly

proof.text: For the dimension assertion apply [pqf-lem-finite-qf] to the now finite structure map $P\to\operatorname{Spec}F$. By [pqf-def-quasifinite] each point is isolated in its fibre. That fibre is $P$ itself, since the unique point of $\operatorname{Spec}F$ has residue field $F$. Thus every singleton of $P$ is open, and every subset is a union of such opens. An irreducible nonempty closed subset can contain only one point: two distinct points would separate it into a singleton and its complement, both open and closed in that subset. Consequently no chain of irreducible closed subsets has a strict inclusion. The definition of topological Krull dimension gives $\dim P\leq0$, including $P=\varnothing$.

source.place: Tag 02NU, lemma-finite-quasi-finite; dimension conclusion from the definition
